name: Wendy Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is used with your name on it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We've got sixty hectares at Mill Lane Farm. About twenty is vegetables, leeks, cabbages, squash, potatoes, and the rest is grass for forty beef cattle. Most of what we grow goes through our farm shop and a vegetable box scheme, where people order online and we deliver on Thursdays. My husband Peter does the tractor work and the cattle, and our daughter Grace runs the shop with me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does your day actually look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I start at six in the packing shed, and the first thing I do is ask the AI assistant to sort the overnight box orders into a picking list by field. It also drafts the newsletter that goes out with the boxes, and I fix the bits that don't sound like me. Then I'm out picking with our two seasonal workers, back in the shop at ten, and out again after lunch. On Sundays we're at church and I don't touch the laptop, that's a family rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, that's a shame, because I've got a lot out of it. But if that's all it ever does, it's still paid its way on this farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like any good tool, it rewards the people who put the work in to learn it. I'd tell the other growers at the market to try the order sorting, because it saves me a good hour every Thursday. I'd not complain that it wasn't more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for us. The business keeps growing slowly, Grace takes on more of the shop, and Peter and I keep going till our late sixties. Nothing in that picture worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, use the AI every day like now, and put our savings into a second polytunnel for early salad, about seven thousand. That pays back in two seasons if the box customers keep coming. And I'd keep pushing Grace to take on the online side fully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Maybe a touch disappointed, I like a bit of excitement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sunday is a no-laptop day. Has that ever been hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once, when the box system crashed on a Saturday night and two hundred orders vanished. Peter said leave it, the Lord rested on the seventh day. I said the Lord didn't have two hundred people expecting leeks, but I left it, and Grace fixed it Monday at five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do your customers say about the AI newsletter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't know. They think it's me, and it mostly is, I fix every line. One lady told me she reads it to her husband at breakfast, so I'd better keep it sounding like Wendy and not like a machine.

S0.say: I'd say it's like any good tool and rewards the people who learn it. I'd tell other growers at the market to try the order sorting because it saves me an hour every Thursday.
S0.think: It's fine for us, because the business keeps growing slowly and our daughter takes on more of the shop. Nothing in that picture worries me.
S0.do: Carries on using AI every day and spends about seven thousand of savings on a second polytunnel for early salad, expecting payback in two seasons. Keeps pushing her daughter to take on the online side fully.
S0.feel: Calm, perhaps a touch disappointed at the lack of excitement.
S0.quote: I said the Lord didn't have two hundred people expecting leeks, but I left it, and Grace fixed it Monday at five.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy blends a daily, confident use of AI with firm family and faith rules, like the Sunday break. She thinks like a small business owner, always looking at payback. She cares that her customers hear her own voice in the newsletter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's exciting, honestly. That's the one where a small, quick farm can beat the big slow ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for anyone willing to work and learn. I'd say farmers should stop waiting for the government to tell them what to do and just get on with it. I'd post that in the growers' group and probably start an argument.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd do well. A robot weeder for the leeks would save us the two seasonal workers' hardest weeks, and the AI already runs half the office. The risk is the supermarkets using the same tools to sell veg cheaper than us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a robot weeder this year, second-hand or leased, maybe twelve thousand, and put the seasonal workers onto picking and the shop. I'd use the time it frees to open a small café in the shop, because people come for the visit as much as the veg. I'd keep learning the AI tools, probably the new stock and pricing one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite excited. A little nervous about the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Twelve thousand is a lot of your savings. How would Peter feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd go quiet and walk round the field twice, that's his way of thinking. Then he'd ask how many months of money we'd have left, and I'd say about two. He'd say fine, but you're telling the bank manager, not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your two seasonal workers?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jakub and Elena. I'd keep them, I'd just move them. They're good people and hard workers, and the café and the shop need hands that can talk to customers, which robots can't do yet.

S1.say: I'd say it's an opportunity for anyone willing to work and learn, and farmers should stop waiting for the government and get on with it. I'd post that in the growers' group and expect an argument.
S1.think: We'd do well, because a robot weeder would cover the hardest weeks for our seasonal workers and AI already runs half the office. The risk is supermarkets using the same tools to sell veg cheaper than us.
S1.do: Buys or leases a robot weeder for about twelve thousand this year and moves the seasonal workers to picking and the shop. Opens a small café in the farm shop with the time saved and learns a new stock and pricing tool.
S1.feel: Calm and excited, a little nervous about the money.
S1.quote: He'd say fine, but you're telling the bank manager, not me.
S1.fieldNote: Wendy would move first and spend savings to do it, and sees steady change as a chance for small farms to beat big ones. Her free-market voice is strong in public, telling farmers not to wait for government. She keeps her workers by moving them to customer-facing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Right. Even I'd say that's too fast. I like change, but that's a landslide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say don't panic and don't wait for a bailout, start doing something today. Small businesses that know their customers will survive. I'd say it confidently, even if I didn't feel completely confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the farming side would stop paying, because robot farms would grow cabbages for pennies. But I don't think people stop wanting to buy from a person they know, so the shop and the boxes might hold. What worries me is Grace, because the shop is her future and I can't promise it'll last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the robots as soon as prices drop, probably in the first year, and cut the field work right down. I'd put everything into the shop, the café and the boxes, the bits where people want a person. And I'd sit down with Grace and make a plan B for her, maybe training in something she can take anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not scared for myself, but for Grace.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would plan B for Grace look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She's good with people and with numbers, so maybe bookkeeping or running events. She'd hate me suggesting it, she loves the shop. But I'd rather she had a second string than nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sound confident but not feel it. What's the gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public, someone has to say it'll be all right, or everyone sells up in a panic. At home, I'd be on the laptop at midnight trying to work out what the robots cost. Peter would bring me cocoa and tell me to come to bed.

S2.say: I'd say don't panic and don't wait for a bailout, start doing something today, because small businesses that know their customers will survive. I'd say it confidently even without feeling fully confident.
S2.think: The farming side would stop paying because robot farms would grow cabbages for pennies, but people may still want to buy from someone they know. What worries me is our daughter, because the shop is her future.
S2.do: Buys robots as soon as prices drop in the first year and cuts field work right down. Puts everything into the shop, café and box scheme, and makes a back-up plan with her daughter, such as training in bookkeeping or events.
S2.feel: Uneasy, not for herself but for her daughter.
S2.quote: In public, someone has to say it'll be all right, or everyone sells up in a panic.
S2.fieldNote: Even the fast scenario leaves Wendy with moves to make, and she bets on the human side of her business. She is honest about a gap between public confidence and late-night worry. Her real concern is her daughter's future, not her own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a good amount of time for a business like ours to turn round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now. Learn the tools, cut costs, find what your customers really value. I'd be saying it at the growers' group and at church, honestly, to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think we'd come out ahead. I'd have the robots in by year two, the café going, and Grace running the shop properly by sixty-three. Then Peter and I could step back and help out on busy days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd lease a robot weeder and try a harvesting robot on the squash. I'd open the café and put Grace in charge of it and the online side. And I'd keep two or three months of money in the bank at all times, because a business that's growing fast can still trip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited. Like the start of a good season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep two or three months in the bank. Why that number?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what got us through the bird flu year, when the egg side we had then went to nothing. Two months saved is the difference between a bad year and a closed farm. I learned that the hard way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your faith fit into how you'd handle all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It keeps me steady, I think. Whatever the machines do, Sunday's still Sunday and we're still at church with our neighbours. That doesn't change, and it matters more when everything else does.

S3.say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start now: learn the tools, cut costs and find what customers value. I'd say it at the growers' group and at church to anyone who'd listen.
S3.think: We'd come out ahead, with robots in by year two, the café going and our daughter running the shop by the time I'm sixty-three. Then my husband and I could step back and help on busy days.
S3.do: Leases a robot weeder and trials a harvesting robot on the squash in the first year. Opens the café with her daughter in charge of it and the online side, and always keeps two or three months of money in the bank.
S3.feel: Calm and a bit excited, like the start of a good season.
S3.quote: Two months saved is the difference between a bad year and a closed farm.
S3.fieldNote: Five years is enough for Wendy to turn the business round, and she sounds energised rather than worried. Her past bad year has taught her to keep a cash cushion even while investing. Faith works for her as a steady point that doesn't move when everything else does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's practically a business plan. I'd be sixty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse, ten years is long enough to learn anything. People who want to work will find a way, and families should help their young ones get ready. I'd say it plainly, because I believe it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this is the best one for us. We'd grow the business slowly, hand it to Grace around sixty-five, and I'd still be in the café making scones because I want to. My only worry is whether there'll be any young people left in the village to buy from us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep investing a bit each year, robots when they're proven and cheap, and grow the café and boxes. I'd help Grace take over the business properly by sixty-five, with her name on the paperwork. And I'd start a little training day for young people on the farm, because someone has to teach them to grow food, robots or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Really quite hopeful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you still want to make scones at sixty-eight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like it, and people come in for a chat, and a robot doesn't ask after your grandchildren. My mother ran a stall at the market till she was seventy-five. It runs in the family, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything make you less hopeful in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the government tried to do it all for people, with handouts instead of jobs. I've seen what that does to a village, people sitting at home. Give folk something to do, that's what I'd want.

S4.say: I'd say there's no excuse, because ten years is long enough to learn anything. People who want to work will find a way, and families should help their young ones get ready.
S4.think: This is the best one for us: grow slowly, hand the business to our daughter around sixty-five and keep baking in the café because I want to. My only worry is whether young people will stay in the village to buy from us.
S4.do: Invests a little each year in robots once proven and cheap and grows the café and box scheme. Hands the business to her daughter by sixty-five and starts training days on the farm for young people.
S4.quote: Because I like it, and people come in for a chat, and a robot doesn't ask after your grandchildren.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Wendy is hopeful and treats it like a business plan. Her traditional views show in wanting jobs and family support rather than handouts. Her picture of herself baking in the café at sixty-eight came from her mother's market stall.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because of Grace. Help for me would be fewer rules on selling direct and running a café on a farm, and cheap loans for small farms to buy robots. And for the young ones, proper apprenticeships, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask people what they'd miss. I'd miss the smell of the packing shed at six in the morning, wet leeks and soil. A machine can pick a leek, but it can't stand in the shed and enjoy that.

headlineQuote: A machine can pick a leek, but it can't stand in the shed and enjoy that.
portrait: Wendy Zhang is a 58-year-old who grows vegetables and runs forty beef cattle on sixty hectares with her husband Peter, selling through a farm shop and a box scheme with their daughter Grace. She uses AI every day to sort orders and draft the customer newsletter, but keeps Sunday laptop-free for church and family. She would buy robots early, move her workers to customer-facing jobs and open a café, and she stays calm in most scenarios. The two-year AGI picture leaves her uneasy, not for herself but for Grace's future in the shop. With five or ten years she sees a chance to grow, hand over to Grace and teach young people to grow food, with work rather than handouts.
biggestWorry: AGI within two years, because of what it would mean for her daughter Grace's future in the shop.
whatWouldHelp: Fewer rules on selling direct and running a farm café, cheap loans for small farms to buy robots, and proper apprenticeships for young people rather than handouts.
